title: Book 5 — Terpsichore, Chapter 77
paragraphs: This army having thus been inglorously broken up, the Athenians after that, wishing to avenge themselves, marched first against the Chalcidians; and the Boeotians came to the Euripus to help the Chalcidians. Seeing the reinforcements, the Athenians resolved first to attack the Boeotians before the Chalcidians. They engaged the Boeotians in battle, and had much the better of them; after killing very many, they took seven hundred of them captive. On this same day the Athenians crossed over into Euboea and engaged the Chalcidians as well; and having conquered these too, they left four thousand allotment-holders on the land belonging to the “Breeders of Horses”—for the wealthier Chalcidians were called Hippobotae, the Breeders of Horses. As many of them as they took captive they kept in confinement together with the captured Boeotians, bound in fetters; and then after a time they let them go, having fixed their ransom at two minae apiece. But the fetters in which they had been bound they hung up on the Acropolis; and these were still there in my time, hanging on walls that had been scorched with fire by the Mede, just opposite the sanctuary that faces west. The tenth part of the ransom they dedicated as an offering, and made of it a bronze four-horse chariot, which stands on the left hand as you enter the Propylaea in the Acropolis, and on it is the following inscription:

“Matched in the deeds of war with the tribes of Boeotia and Chalcis, the sons of Athens prevailed, conquered and tamed them in fight: in chains of iron and darkness they quenched their insolent spirit, and to Athena present these, a tithe of the ransom they paid.”
